lessons.title: Follow inherited descriptors
lessons.reading: Read a few paragraphs of the Processes section. Stop when the relationship between a parent and child gives you a question.
lessons.summary: A launcher opens a file, forks, and the child executes a helper. What access might the helper still have?
lessons.prompt: A launcher opens a file, forks, and the child executes a helper. What access might the helper still have?
explanation: The parent creates a tiny demo file and keeps an open descriptor: a small integer naming its access to that file. The child can keep that access, close its own entry, or mark the entry to close when it loads the helper. The helper attempts to read the known demo bytes; the parent separately checks its own entry.

After fork, the two processes have distinct descriptor-table entries referring to the same open-file description, the kernel-managed record behind the open file. Closing one entry removes that reference. FD_CLOEXEC instead requests closure during successful exec. The code walkthrough separates these operations and their failure cases.
After following the program, ask which access was actually removed. The helper retains its credentials and any other surviving access; losing this one descriptor does not establish a sandbox.
lessons.follow_up: If the parent closes its copy after fork, which process still has a reference to the open file?
lessons.boundary: The application calls fork and execl through its C library. The indexed calls below are inside the kernel. The connection across those layers is a curated explanation, not a compiler-resolved edge from the experiment.

experiment.intro: An optional experiment using a temporary, immediately unlinked file containing only “demo only”. No privileges or sensitive files are involved.
experiment.expected:
default: helper inherited descriptor=yes data=demo only
--cloexec: helper inherited descriptor=no
--close-child: helper inherited descriptor=no
all three: parent descriptor still open=yes
experiment.observe: Compare what the helper can read with whether the parent’s descriptor remains open. The closed descriptor is one piece of state, not a general clean slate.
experiment.assumptions: One single-threaded parent and one helper; a tiny regular file containing demo text. No sensitive file is used. Run the supplied ./ command without moving or renaming the executable mid-run.
experiment.variation: Run the unchanged complete program once normally, once with --cloexec, and once with --close-child. Both optional arguments change the child/helper path while leaving the parent descriptor observation available.
experiment.variability: Descriptor numbers and PIDs vary. Short regular-file transfers cause explicit diagnostics; this is not a general-purpose buffered reader.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.

The file is unlinked immediately after creation. Normal paths close descriptor entries; the parent collects its owned child. If unlink itself fails, inspect only the generated /tmp/kse-authority-* demo path.

checkpoints.notice: The new task’s file setup is delegated to copy_files. Read the call and its error branch.

reading.callee: Sets up the new task’s table of open-file descriptor entries.
reading.statement: copy_process delegates file-table setup to copy_files.
reading.inputs: clone_flags selects creation options; p is the new task; args->no_files supplies the request’s no-files choice.
reading.result: retval is checked immediately; a nonzero result takes a cleanup branch.

checkpoints.title: A copied table can retain shared references
checkpoints.notice: Read the CLONE_FILES branch and the later dup_fd call. Ordinary fork takes the table-duplication path; sharing a whole table is a separate option.
checkpoints.ignore: The helper’s allocation mechanics are not needed for this question.
checkpoints.question: How is sharing a table different from two tables pointing to the same open file?

reading.caller: Sets up the new task’s table of open-file descriptor entries.
reading.callee: Creates a separate descriptor table, retaining references to existing open files.
reading.statement: copy_files calls dup_fd after the whole-table-sharing branch.
reading.inputs: oldf is the existing file-table context. NULL supplies no punch-hole range for this duplication. Ordinary fork does not request CLONE_FILES.
reading.result: IS_ERR checks the returned pointer for an encoded kernel error. On success tsk->files receives newf.
reading.syntax: A pointer is a value locating an object. IS_ERR/PTR_ERR are kernel conventions, different from libc’s -1/errno convention.

checkpoints.title: The close-on-exec checkpoint
checkpoints.notice: This call handles descriptors marked to close during exec. Inspect the surrounding comments.
checkpoints.ignore: Credential transitions and binary-format dispatch are separate topics.
checkpoints.question: Why can an unmarked descriptor still be useful to the replacement program?

reading.caller: Carries out core state transitions during program replacement.
reading.callee: Closes entries marked close-on-exec in the supplied descriptor-table context.
reading.statement: begin_new_exec calls do_close_on_exec with this task’s files context.
reading.inputs: me->files selects the current task’s file-table context. The preceding comment places this after the point of no return and table unsharing.
reading.result: There is no return value tested at this call. Later replacement work continues; this line alone does not inventory all retained access.
reading.syntax: A call used as a statement can perform work without assigning a result. FD_CLOEXEC applies to descriptor entries; losing one entry does not revoke other references.

walkthrough.title: Interfaces and types
explanation: Feature-test macros request declarations before headers. ssize_t can carry -1 or a byte count; size_t represents object sizes. errno is interpreted only according to the operation that failed.
walkthrough.question: Why are byte counts not stored in an unsigned type here?
walkthrough.situation: A launcher will give a new program access to an owned demo file through a descriptor.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A descriptor is a small integer naming an entry in this process’s open-resource table. It is not the bytes of the file or a pathname. A function argument is an input value. A pointer locates storage; argv locates the pointers to this invocation’s argument strings.
steps: #define _POSIX_C_SOURCE requests POSIX declarations before any header is read.
fcntl.h declares descriptor flag interfaces; stdlib.h declares conversion and temporary-file creation; sys/wait.h declares child-status interfaces.
main receives argc, the number of argument strings, and argv, a way to find those strings.
walkthrough.change: Removing the feature-test macro can hide declarations on some library configurations; it does not disable a kernel feature.

walkthrough.title: Read the descriptor argument carefully
explanation: argc and strcmp select helper mode. strtol parses base-10 text, checks errno, and returns an end pointer. *end dereferences that pointer to ensure no trailing characters remain. The checked range makes the later int cast safe. A zero-filled array leaves room for a C-string terminator.
walkthrough.question: Why would atoi hide a malformed descriptor argument?
walkthrough.situation: After exec the helper receives a descriptor number as text. It must validate that text before using the number.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A C string is characters followed by a zero byte. char * names a pointer to characters; a pointer can identify the beginning of a string. A function argument is an input to a call.
steps: Check argc before accessing argv[1] or argv[2]. && stops before later tests if the count is wrong.
strtol reads decimal text. &end supplies an address where strtol stores the pointer to the first unconverted character.
Reset errno before conversion, then reject range errors, empty text, trailing characters, and values outside int range. *end reads the character at that pointer.
After those checks, (int)number safely converts the descriptor. char data[32] = {0} creates a zero-filled character array.
read receives the descriptor, the array’s starting address, and a maximum count. -1 is failure; EBADF means this entry is unavailable. A short successful read is a different diagnostic.
The nine expected bytes leave a zero terminator for %s. strcmp verifies their contents before the helper reports success.
walkthrough.change: Skipping numeric validation can confuse invalid input with a valid descriptor. This bounded example expects one tiny regular-file read; it is not a general streaming read loop.

walkthrough.title: Create only demo data
explanation: mkstemp creates a unique regular file; unlink removes its name immediately. Write errors and short counts are diagnosed separately. This finite example expects exactly nine bytes, then seeks to the beginning.
walkthrough.question: Does removing the pathname remove an already-open descriptor?
walkthrough.situation: The parent creates only its own file, writes demo bytes, and resets its position before inheritance.
walkthrough.prerequisite: An array holds several elements. A writable name array lets mkstemp replace XXXXXX with a unique suffix. A byte count is a number of transferred bytes, not a success flag.
steps: mkstemp creates a fresh file and returns its descriptor; check -1 before using it.
unlink removes the file’s name. The open descriptor still keeps the file object alive.
write must return nine for this tiny regular-file example. Handle -1 with perror and a shorter nonnegative count with an explicit message.
lseek sets the shared open-file position to zero so the helper can read from the beginning. Failure paths close the descriptor.
walkthrough.change: Omitting lseek leaves the position after the written bytes: the helper could encounter EOF rather than the expected data.

walkthrough.title: Set one descriptor flag
explanation: F_GETFD reads descriptor flags; flags | FD_CLOEXEC preserves other bits while adding close-on-exec. || short-circuits so an invalid flag value is not applied. This single-threaded example deliberately separates creation and flag setting; multithreaded launchers should consider atomic O_CLOEXEC creation.
walkthrough.question: Which object owns this flag: the descriptor entry or the shared file description?
walkthrough.situation: The optional --cloexec choice marks this descriptor to close during successful exec.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A flag is a named bit in an integer. Bitwise | combines selected bits, unlike logical ||, which combines true/false tests.
steps: Check the argument count before comparing the option string.
F_GETFD retrieves existing descriptor flags. Check its failure before attempting the update.
flags | FD_CLOEXEC preserves old bits and sets close-on-exec. F_SETFD applies those descriptor flags.
walkthrough.change: Without FD_CLOEXEC the default branch retains this descriptor across exec. Close-on-exec does not close the parent’s entry or prohibit reopening an accessible file.

walkthrough.title: Choose the child preparation
explanation: The parent sees a positive child PID. The zero-return branch can close only its own descriptor entry before exec. A failure path uses _exit so it does not run the parent program’s cleanup twice.
walkthrough.question: What reference remains if only the child closes its descriptor?
walkthrough.situation: Parent and child need different work: only the child prepares to become the helper.
walkthrough.prerequisite: fork returns -1 on failure, zero in the child, and the child PID in the parent. Both successful paths continue after the same call.
steps: Store fork’s result in pid_t child_pid so later branches can identify their paths.
Handle -1 by reporting and closing the existing descriptor.
Inside the zero branch, the --close-child option closes only this child’s entry before exec. A failed close ends this child with _exit(1).
walkthrough.change: Closing in the child does not remove the parent’s descriptor entry. The inherited entries initially refer to the same open-file description.

walkthrough.title: Convert and pass an argument
explanation: snprintf writes decimal digits into a bounded array and reports the required length. execl receives a pathname, new argument strings and a terminating (char *)NULL. Run the supplied ./ command so argv[0] is a usable path.
walkthrough.question: Why can the child pass the descriptor number as text without transferring the file contents?
walkthrough.situation: The helper expects text arguments, so the child must turn the integer descriptor into text.
walkthrough.prerequisite: snprintf writes formatted text into a bounded character array and returns the required character count, excluding its terminating zero. A cast explicitly converts a type after range checks.
steps: descriptor reserves 32 characters. %d formats fd into that array; sizeof supplies its capacity.
Check a negative result first. Then cast the nonnegative length to size_t and reject a result at least as large as the buffer, which indicates truncation.
execl takes the executable pathname and individual string arguments, including the new argv[0]. The --helper marker selects the helper branch on its new invocation.
(char *)NULL supplies a null pointer of the required type to end this variable-argument list. It is not an empty string.
Only failure returns from execl; perror and _exit(1) handle that path.
walkthrough.change: Omitting the null sentinel makes the variable-argument call invalid. Use the documented ./ path because execl does not search PATH here.

walkthrough.title: Observe without inferring complete isolation
explanation: The parent waits, reports its own descriptor state and releases its reference. Helper behavior depends on descriptor survival through exec. A failed read with EBADF is evidence about that entry, not proof of denied access through every other path.
walkthrough.question: Could the helper still read some other file using its unchanged credentials?
walkthrough.situation: The parent waits until the helper is finished, then checks and releases its own descriptor.
walkthrough.prerequisite: Encoded wait status must be classified before extracting a normal exit code. An address such as &status lets waitpid fill storage.
steps: Retry waitpid only for EINTR; other errors report and close the parent’s descriptor.
fcntl with F_GETFD observes whether the parent entry remains usable. The conditional operator condition ? yes : no chooses the printed word.
close releases this parent entry.
The final || expression stops if WIFEXITED is false, so WEXITSTATUS is used only for normal termination.
walkthrough.change: A helper that lacks this descriptor might still open other paths under its credentials. This experiment tests descriptor inheritance, not complete isolation.

lessons.title: What does a process ID identify?
lessons.reading: Use Chapter 2 for the broad idea. When you reach Chapter 6, compare a program’s identity with the state the kernel tracks for it.
lessons.summary: If two executions run the same program, what makes them different processes?
lessons.prompt: If two executions run the same program, what makes them different processes?
explanation: This running program asks Linux for its own process ID and its current parent’s ID, stores those numbers, and prints them. A process is one running execution with its own identity and state; the program is the executable code and data that it runs. This example creates no child.

In Linux, a task is a schedulable execution context. Threads add a distinction: getpid returns a thread-group ID, while gettid identifies the calling thread. You can leave thread details until the relevant reading.
A PID is an identifier. Access control depends on additional state; possessing a new number is not an isolation mechanism.
lessons.follow_up: After a successful exec, would you expect the PID to change? Keep that prediction for the program-replacement topic.
lessons.boundary: getpid in the C program is an application-facing interface. The macro-generated kernel handler is a separate layer. This index covers the kernel, not the C library wrapper.

experiment.intro: Print the current process ID and its parent’s ID. Repeat the command if you are curious.
experiment.expected:
pid=<a process ID> parent=<its parent’s ID>
pid=<another process ID> parent=<its parent’s ID>
experiment.observe: Values depend on the running system. Repeated invocations often share a parent. PID reuse is possible over time.
experiment.assumptions: A normal Linux process with a parent visible in its PID namespace. No new process or namespace is created by this example.
experiment.variation: Run the unchanged program twice from the same shell. Observe actual IDs; do not require a particular numeric PID. This is a runtime comparison and needs no code changes.
experiment.variability: PIDs vary and may be reused over time. The current parent can change through reparenting; getppid may validly be zero when that parent is outside this process’s PID namespace.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.
This program creates no child, file or directory. It only observes IDs and checks its output result.

reading.inputs: current identifies the calling task. getpid exposes its thread-group identity, which differs from gettid for other threads in a group.
reading.result: return sends the helper’s value back through the kernel handler. This is not a permission check.
reading.syntax: SYSCALL_DEFINE0(getpid) generates this build’s __arm64_sys_getpid name. The zero denotes no syscall arguments; users need not memorize the generated name.

next.question: What sort of kernel record holds task state?

checkpoints.title: A task has a kernel record
checkpoints.notice: This structure is the kernel’s task record. Its size is a reason to follow one field or responsibility at a time.
checkpoints.ignore: You do not need to read or memorize this entire structure.
checkpoints.question: Which kinds of state would you expect a task record to refer to?

reading.caller: Defines the kernel’s task record and references to task state.
reading.statement: struct task_struct begins a type definition, not a function call.
reading.inputs: Its fields describe or refer to parts of task state; configuration controls which fields are present.
reading.result: A type definition produces no runtime return value. Follow one field only when you have a question about it.
reading.syntax: struct defines a record with named fields. #ifdef includes fields conditionally while compiling this configuration.

walkthrough.title: Find declarations
explanation: stdio.h declares printf; unistd.h declares the process interfaces. Including a header makes the compiler aware of a contract; it does not call into the kernel.
walkthrough.question: Which header would you consult for getppid?
walkthrough.situation: One existing process will print two IDs; this program creates no child.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A header supplies declarations so the compiler knows interface names and their types.
steps: #include <stdio.h> makes output declarations available.
#include <unistd.h> makes getpid and getppid declarations available. Including it does not call either function.
walkthrough.change: Removing unistd.h loses the declarations; it does not prevent the process from having an identity.

walkthrough.title: Types, calls, and casts
explanation: getppid can validly return zero when the parent lies outside the caller’s PID namespace. Process IDs are identifiers within a namespace, not credentials.
walkthrough.question: Why must the format placeholder match the argument type?
walkthrough.situation: The process asks for its own ID and its current parent ID, then keeps the results.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A call returns a value. A declaration names storage for that value; = supplies its initial value. An integer cast explicitly converts a number to another integer type.
steps: long process_id declares integer storage named process_id.
getpid() requests this process’s ID. (long) converts its pid_t result to match the later %ld output format.
The second declaration does the same for getppid(), naming the current parent. These are two observations, not an atomic snapshot.
walkthrough.change: Swapping the calls swaps what the names contain. A parent can exit and reparenting can change a later parent-ID observation.

walkthrough.title: Format the observation
explanation: The first %ld consumes process_id and the second consumes parent_id. A negative printf return signals an output failure. Numeric IDs vary across executions and can be reused after a process lifetime ends.
walkthrough.question: Would the same numeric PID tomorrow prove this is the same process?
walkthrough.situation: The stored numbers become one readable line.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A format string contains literal text and placeholders. Each placeholder must agree with the type of its corresponding argument.
steps: printf takes the string first, then process_id and parent_id in that order. Each %ld consumes one long value.
A negative printf result means output failure. The if body reports it and returns 1.
return 0 reports success only after that check; this program has no temporary file or child to clean up.
walkthrough.change: Changing %ld to an incompatible format is a C type mismatch, not merely a cosmetic change.

lessons.title: Lab 001: Follow a fork call
lessons.reference: Chapter 2 companion Lab 001 · deeper reading: Chapter 24, §24.2.2
lessons.reading: When you reach fork, read its return-value behavior and memory semantics. This is a later-reading option, not a prerequisite for continuing Chapter 2.
lessons.summary: Trace one fork call, its return value, and the two branches of a small program.
lessons.prompt: An integer starts at 42. The child assigns 7 after fork. What will each process print, and which return value sends it down that branch?
explanation: The original process starts with an integer named value containing 42. After successful fork, the parent and child both continue after that call. The child takes the zero-result branch, assigns 7 to its own ordinary variable and prints it. The parent waits for that child to finish, then prints its own value, still 42.

Choose Read the C code to unpack the variable, function call and branches one statement at a time. The optional deeper explanation there distinguishes this private variable from explicit shared memory and explains why copy-on-write is not needed to follow the basic behavior.
lessons.follow_up: Why can the virtual addresses match even though later values differ?
lessons.boundary: The C library’s fork wrapper is outside this index. These checkpoints investigate kernel memory setup; they do not trace an observed run of the experiment.

experiment.intro: The parent waits so the two output lines have a predictable order.
experiment.observe: Compare the assignment in the child branch with the value printed in the parent branch.
experiment.assumptions: Single-threaded ordinary fork; an ordinary local int, not a shared-memory mapping. A normal Linux shell and a C compiler are sufficient.
experiment.variation: Replace only value = 7; in the child branch with value = 99;. Recompile the complete file. Compare child value=99 with the unchanged parent value=42.
experiment.variability: PIDs and scheduling vary, but waitpid deliberately orders the displayed child line before the parent line. The fixed integer output follows from this program, not from arbitrary concurrent printf ordering.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.
The parent collects its owned child. There are no temporary files or directories. The child flushes its message before _exit.

checkpoints.title: Creation delegates memory setup
checkpoints.notice: Read the memory-setup call and the failure check.
checkpoints.ignore: Other resource-copying calls are separate responsibilities.
checkpoints.question: What needs to succeed before creation continues?

reading.caller: Prepares a new task (a kernel execution record) and its memory, file and other resource state.
reading.callee: Chooses whether the new task shares or duplicates the record describing its memory.
reading.statement: copy_process calls copy_mm and stores its result in retval.
reading.inputs: clone_flags carries creation choices; p identifies the new task being prepared.
reading.result: The following if (retval) branches to cleanup when setup reports failure. Creation has more work afterward.
reading.syntax: Arguments are inputs between parentheses. = stores the call result; the following if tests it. The kernel convention here uses zero for success.

next.question: Which branch duplicates the memory context for ordinary fork?

steps: copy_process is preparing a new task: the kernel’s record of an execution context. Other creation work surrounds this call.

copy_mm(clone_flags, p) calls another function to set up memory. The values inside parentheses are its arguments: clone_flags carries creation choices; p is a pointer identifying the new task being prepared.
The call returns an integer status. retval = stores that result in an existing variable; this is assignment, not a comparison.

Here zero means success; a negative error code means failure. The following if (retval) tests for a nonzero result and goto bad_fork_cleanup_signal sends failures to cleanup. This internal kernel convention is different from userspace fork returning -1 and setting errno.
On success, creation continues with other setup. The compiler arrow establishes this call site, not that it executed in your experiment. Next, examine the choice inside copy_mm.

prerequisites.title: What does a pointer identify?
prerequisites.text: A pointer is a value identifying an object in memory. Here p identifies a task record. Passing that pointer lets the called function work with the same record; the record is not copied just because the pointer is passed.

checkpoints.title: Sharing or duplicating the memory context
checkpoints.notice: Read the CLONE_VM condition and the else branch containing dup_mm.
checkpoints.ignore: Page-table details inside helpers can wait.
checkpoints.question: Which branch fits the experiment’s ordinary fork?

reading.caller: Chooses whether the new task shares or duplicates the record describing its memory.
reading.callee: Creates a new memory-management record based on the existing one.
reading.statement: In the else branch, copy_mm calls dup_mm and keeps the returned pointer in mm.
reading.inputs: The earlier CLONE_VM test distinguishes shared context from this duplication path. tsk is the new task; current->mm is the calling task’s context.
reading.result: A null mm result returns -ENOMEM. Later assignments attach the resulting context to the new task.
reading.syntax: -> selects a field through a pointer. !mm tests for a null pointer here. This is not yet a page-by-page copy-on-write walkthrough.

prerequisites.title: Records, fields, and the arrow in current->mm
prerequisites.text: A structure is a record with named parts called fields. A pointer identifies a record; -> selects a field through that pointer. current->mm reads the mm field of the task executing this code. tsk->mm = mm writes a field of the new task.

prerequisites.title: Binary & versus an address such as &status
prerequisites.text: With two operands, a & b combines their bits. With one operand, &status obtains the address of status. The number of operands changes the meaning; the flag test here has two.

prerequisites.title: A null pointer and two kinds of return value
prerequisites.text: NULL is a null pointer: it identifies no object. !mm is true when mm is null. dup_mm returns a pointer to a record or NULL; copy_mm instead returns an integer status, zero or a negative error code. Neither result here is the userspace fork PID.

names: The caller passes p as the second argument; copy_mm names that same new-task pointer tsk. Caller and callee do not need the same variable name.
The task executing this kernel code, not the new task being prepared.
In copy_mm, the executing task’s existing memory-management record (current->mm).
In copy_mm, the memory-management record being selected for the new task.
In copy_process, the integer status returned by copy_mm.

groups.title: Existing memory
steps: copy_mm receives the new-task pointer as tsk. This is the caller’s p under a different parameter name.
current identifies the task executing this code. current->mm reads its memory-management record; -> selects a named part (a field) through a pointer. oldmm = current->mm stores that pointer in oldmm.
Our ordinary userspace process has a memory context. The earlier !oldmm return handles a different case, such as a kernel thread.

groups.title: Sharing requested?
steps: Flags encode individual choices as bits (binary digits). CLONE_VM names the memory-sharing bit.
In clone_flags & CLONE_VM, binary & keeps bits present in both values. This tests bits; unary & in &status instead obtains an address.
A nonzero result selects the sharing branch: mmget retains a reference and mm = oldmm selects the existing record.

Ordinary fork does not request CLONE_VM, so its relevant path is else. This is an authored connection supported by the fork/clone interface contracts and this source, not a compiler-resolved edge from our C program.

groups.title: Separate context
steps: mm = dup_mm(tsk, current->mm) asks for a new memory-management record and stores the returned pointer in mm. The helper’s source comment documents a pointer to the duplicated record on success, or NULL on failure. NULL is a null pointer: it identifies no object.
if (!mm) tests for that null pointer and returns -ENOMEM on failure. Otherwise tsk->mm = mm and tsk->active_mm = mm attach the selected record to the new task.
The final return 0 reports copy_mm’s integer success status. That status is different from the pointer returned by dup_mm.
This shows context selection and its failure handling. It does not show eager copying of every physical page or the complete copy-on-write implementation.

flow.title: Private copies and explicit shared memory
flow.scope: Ordinary private mappings separate after fork; MAP_SHARED regions remain shared according to their mapping contract.

nodes.label: Parent calls fork
nodes.detail: Failure creates no child. On success parent and child continue with distinct fork return values.

nodes.label: Parent private int
nodes.detail: An ordinary local int belongs to the parent’s private state; copy-on-write can implement its independent writes.

nodes.label: Child private int
nodes.detail: The child’s ordinary private int can be changed without overwriting the parent’s int.

nodes.label: Parent explicit MAP_SHARED region
nodes.detail: This is a different region from the ordinary private int. Its mapping refers to shared backing.

nodes.label: Child inherited MAP_SHARED region
nodes.detail: An explicit shared mapping can remain a reference to the same backing after fork.

nodes.label: Common shared backing
nodes.detail: Shared visibility still needs synchronization and a lifetime protocol. It does not remove other process authority.

walkthrough.title: Headers and the first variable
explanation: Headers supply declarations, including pid_t and waitpid. main(void) says this function takes no arguments. int value = 42 declares storage and initializes it; it is not an instruction to the kernel to share that storage.
walkthrough.question: Which names in this segment are types, functions, and variables?
walkthrough.situation: One running program needs a place to keep the number 42 before it creates a child.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A variable is a named place for a value. A type tells C what kind of value belongs there. A declaration introduces the name; an initializer supplies its first value.
steps: #include asks the C preprocessor to read declarations from a header. A declaration tells the compiler how a named interface can be called.
int main(void) defines the starting function: int is its result type; void says this version takes no arguments. The braces enclose its statements.
int value = 42; introduces value as an integer and initializes it to 42. The semicolon ends the declaration.
stdio.h declares output interfaces; unistd.h declares fork and _exit; sys/wait.h declares waiting interfaces; errno.h supplies error information. Headers do not themselves create a process.
walkthrough.change: Changing 42 changes the starting number. Removing a needed header removes declarations the compiler needs; it is not a way to avoid using the kernel.

walkthrough.title: The fork call and its three return cases
explanation: POSIX specifies the different fork return values. A PID identifies a process; it does not prove that process has fewer permissions.

This example has one thread and an ordinary private integer. Linux commonly implements private-memory duplication with copy-on-write: initially shared physical pages can be copied when written. That implementation detail is unnecessary for following the two return paths.
Explicit shared mappings are a contrasting case. Their writes can be visible between processes; the private-variable example makes no claim about them.
walkthrough.question: Which process can use child_pid as the ID of its child?
walkthrough.situation: The original process reaches one call. The next statements must distinguish creation failure, the child path, and the parent path.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A function call requests work using the name followed by parentheses. A return value is the value that the call gives back to the expression containing it. It can be stored and compared.
steps: child_pid names a variable. It will let the following statements remember this call’s result.
pid_t is a system-provided type suitable for process IDs. It is a type name, not a call or a particular PID.
fork() calls the process-creation interface. The empty parentheses supply no arguments.
The call produces a return value. In this declaration, = initializes child_pid with that value; it is not the == comparison operator.
On success, parent and child both continue after this call. The parent receives the positive child PID; the child receives zero. Neither restarts main().

if (child_pid == -1) compares the value with the failure value. Its braces contain the failure path. perror reports a diagnostic from errno, the error number recorded for that failed interface call; return 1 ends this invocation unsuccessfully.
The next segment tests zero to select the child’s work. Only the parent reaches the later wait after the child’s _exit.
walkthrough.change: Removing the failure branch could send the program into parent work when no child exists. Changing == to = in a condition would assign a value instead of comparing it.

walkthrough.title: The child branch and formatted output
explanation: The == operator compares, while = assigns. Only the process whose fork return is zero enters this branch. %d requires an int argument. fflush sends the user-space output buffer onward before _exit ends execution without stdio cleanup.
walkthrough.question: Why is comparing child_pid to zero different from assigning zero to it?
walkthrough.situation: The child has reached the zero branch. It changes its own value, prints it, and ends so it cannot run the parent’s work.
walkthrough.prerequisite: An assignment replaces an existing variable’s value. A string is text in double quotes. printf may first place output in a library buffer in this process’s memory instead of immediately writing it to the destination.
steps: if (child_pid == 0) selects the child. Its braces keep the following statements together.
value = 7; assigns to the already declared value; it does not introduce another variable.
printf receives a format string and value as arguments: arguments are the inputs between parentheses, separated by commas. %d formats an int; \n requests a newline.

stdout names the C standard-output stream; it may lead to a terminal or a redirected file. fflush(stdout) sends its pending bytes toward that destination. This is needed here because _exit bypasses ordinary stdio cleanup.
EOF is a named stdio constant used as this flush interface’s failure result. Compare the returned value with EOF before proceeding. On failure _exit(1) reports unsuccessful child completion.
_exit(0) ends the child immediately with success status. The parent keeps running independently.
walkthrough.change: Without _exit the child could fall into code intended for the parent. Without a successful flush, buffered output can be lost, especially when output is redirected.

walkthrough.title: The parent waits and decodes
explanation: &status supplies the address of an int that waitpid can fill. Its returned PID is separate from that encoded status. EINTR means retry this wait. || short-circuits, so WEXITSTATUS is used only after WIFEXITED says a normal exit code exists.
walkthrough.question: Which value answers who changed state, and which answers how it ended?
walkthrough.situation: The parent needs to know that its child finished before it prints the final observation.
walkthrough.prerequisite: int status reserves integer storage. &status means the address of that storage. A pointer is a value identifying storage; passing this address lets waitpid write into the parent’s integer. The integer’s contents and its address are different things.
steps: waitpid(child_pid, &status, 0) names this child, supplies where to put completion information, and requests ordinary blocking waiting with option 0.
The return value says which child was collected, or -1 on failure. The encoded information written into status is a separate output.
while repeats its braced body while the comparison is true. If errno is EINTR, a signal interrupted waiting; continue retries. Other errors report and return without reading status.
WIFEXITED(status) asks whether normal exit occurred. Only that variant has a normal exit code to extract.
! reverses a true/false test. || means OR and stops when its left side is true. Therefore WEXITSTATUS is reached only after WIFEXITED was true.
A nonzero child exit code makes this experiment fail. Waiting orders the observation; it does not cause the child’s variable assignment.
walkthrough.change: Without waiting, the output order could change and completion would not be collected. Removing the variant check would treat signal-termination information as a normal exit code.

walkthrough.title: Inspect the parent and finish
explanation: The child has finished before this print. The ordinary int is in private process memory: the child assignment does not overwrite the parent variable. This statement does not cover explicitly shared mappings. return 0 reports success from the parent program.
walkthrough.question: Would a MAP_SHARED integer obey the same independence rule?
walkthrough.situation: The parent has collected successful child completion and now prints its own integer.
walkthrough.prerequisite: Returning from main reports this invocation’s exit status. It does not return a value to the child. Normal return also performs ordinary stdio cleanup.
steps: printf reads the parent’s value and substitutes it for %d. The earlier child assignment operated in the child’s private memory.
return 0 ends the parent successfully. The closing brace ends main; it belongs to the complete program, not a second execution path.
walkthrough.change: Changing only this format string changes the report, not the stored integer. Changing value here changes the parent’s value after the child has already finished.

containment.subject: The forked child
containment.resource: An ordinary integer in private process memory
containment.origin: Inherited initial memory contents at fork
containment.enforcement: Separate virtual address spaces, commonly implemented with copy-on-write
containment.remaining: The child still inherits credentials and open descriptors; private variables do not remove file or network authority.
containment.establishes: Establishes independence for this ordinary int. It does not test shared mappings, credential restrictions, or syscall filtering.

explorer_start.question: What happens when my program creates a child?
explorer_start.situation: Your C program calls fork(), then branches on its return value.
explorer_start.establishes: See where task creation delegates memory setup and checks whether it succeeded.
explorer_start.prerequisite: Understand one variable, a function call and an if branch; Lab 001 introduces each.
explorer_start.purpose: How Linux prepares the child’s memory context
explorer_start.introduction: Your C program calls fork(). Here we start inside copy_process, a kernel helper, to examine one responsibility: preparing the new task’s memory context. This is not a trace through the C library and syscall boundary. Follow two reviewed checkpoints, with optional full-definition detours, then connect them to the private-variable experiment.

guided_path.title: Preparing the child’s memory context
guided_path.connection_title: Connect the result back to the C experiment
connection: We saw copy_process delegate memory setup to copy_mm and check its integer status before continuing creation.

Inside copy_mm we examined the choice between sharing an existing memory context and preparing a separate one. Ordinary fork does not request CLONE_VM, so the duplication branch is the relevant path for our single-threaded C program.

Together with the fork interface contract, this supports the private-variable model: the child can change its ordinary int from 42 to 7 without updating the parent’s int. This is an authored connection to the C experiment, not a compiler-resolved edge or an observation of that experiment running.

We have not inspected all copy-on-write machinery, explicit shared mappings, or every inherited resource. Separate private memory does not establish a complete sandbox: credentials and open descriptors still matter.
guided_path.definition: A memory context is the kernel’s bookkeeping describing a process’s memory—not the contents of an individual C variable.

lessons.title: Follow two file descriptors
lessons.reading: Read the file-sharing discussion when it fits your reading. Compare descriptor-table entries with open-file descriptions.
lessons.summary: The child reads the first two bytes of a file. After waiting, which byte will the parent read through its inherited descriptor?
lessons.prompt: The child reads the first two bytes of a file. After waiting, which byte will the parent read through its inherited descriptor?
explanation: The parent writes abcd into a tiny file and puts its reading position at the start. The child reads two bytes and ends. After waiting for that child, the parent reads one byte and observes c: its read begins where the child left the shared position.

Each process has its own descriptor entry, but these inherited entries refer to the same open-file description. That kernel-managed record holds the current offset, meaning the byte position for the next ordinary read. The child’s read advances that shared position.

Waiting makes the child’s read happen before the parent’s read. Two independent open calls would instead create separate open-file descriptions. This example assumes one thread per process, a blocking regular file and a tiny finite transfer.
lessons.follow_up: What would you predict if the child opened the pathname independently instead?
lessons.boundary: These are compiler-resolved calls inside the kernel. The explanation linking descriptor references to the experiment is a teaching annotation, not a runtime trace.

experiment.intro: Use a temporary, unlinked four-byte file. The child reads two bytes before the parent reads one.
experiment.observe: A parent result of c follows the child’s read of a and b. Both processes close their own descriptors.
experiment.assumptions: An unlinked regular file with four demo bytes, one parent and one child, and no other writers. Short transfers are reported explicitly rather than handled as a general streaming-copy implementation.
experiment.variation: Change char first[2] to char first[1], the corresponding count != 2 check to count != 1, and the diagnostic text "two regular-file bytes" to "one regular-file byte". Keep sizeof(first) as the read size. Recompile; the parent should next read b.
experiment.variability: The descriptor number varies and is not printed. Waiting removes scheduling variation from which byte the parent sees.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.
The temporary file is unlinked while open. Both processes close their entries; the parent collects the child. Unexpected short transfers fail this bounded regular-file experiment.

checkpoints.title: Follow descriptor-table duplication
checkpoints.notice: The dup_fd call duplicates the table for this path.
checkpoints.ignore: CLONE_FILES is a distinct sharing option; ordinary fork does not request it.
checkpoints.question: Does a new table imply new open-file descriptions?

reading.caller: Sets up the new task’s table of open-file descriptor entries.
reading.callee: Creates a separate descriptor table, retaining references to existing open files.
reading.statement: The new table is obtained through dup_fd; a new table alone does not establish new open-file descriptions.
reading.inputs: oldf is the existing table context. The earlier CLONE_FILES branch instead retains the whole table.
reading.result: On success the new task’s files field receives newf; encoded pointer errors are returned before assignment.
reading.syntax: IS_ERR recognizes a kernel error encoded in a pointer. It does not mean every non-null pointer is failure.

next.question: Where are existing file objects retained?

checkpoints.title: Inspect what duplication retains
checkpoints.notice: Read the get_file call and the neighboring assignment into the new table. The code retains a reference to an existing file object.
checkpoints.ignore: The surrounding allocation and resizing mechanics can wait.
checkpoints.question: Which objects are retained by reference?

reading.caller: Creates a separate descriptor table, retaining references to existing open files.
reading.callee: Keeps an additional counted reference to an already open file object.
reading.statement: For a non-null file entry, dup_fd calls get_file(f), then assigns f into the new descriptor table.
reading.inputs: f is the existing struct file pointer. The neighboring loop reads old entries and populates new ones.
reading.result: get_file returns the same file pointer; this statement ignores that return value. Its important effect retains a counted reference, and the later assignment stores f in the new table. It does not open the pathname again or create an independent file position.
reading.syntax: if (f) selects a present entry. The assignments are pointer references, not a copy of the file’s contents.

flow.title: Two entries, one open file description
flow.scope: Assume fd B is produced by dup(A), not an independent open.

nodes.label: Descriptor A: its own FD_CLOEXEC
nodes.detail: Descriptor flags belong to this entry. Changing its close-on-exec flag does not set the other entry’s flag.

nodes.label: Descriptor B: its own FD_CLOEXEC
nodes.detail: dup creates a second entry referring to the existing description; it does not independently reopen the pathname.

nodes.label: One open file description
nodes.detail: The kernel open state is shared by these two references.

nodes.label: Shared offset and status flags
nodes.detail: A read through either entry can advance this offset. O_APPEND and similar status flags belong to the description.

nodes.label: Underlying file object
nodes.detail: The file object and the per-open description are different objects.

walkthrough.title: Feature-test macro and declarations
explanation: Define _POSIX_C_SOURCE before headers so the requested POSIX declarations are exposed. A feature-test macro selects declarations; it does not enable a kernel security feature.
walkthrough.question: Why must this define precede the headers?
walkthrough.situation: Two processes will read a single tiny file in a controlled order.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A feature-test macro requests library declarations; it must precede the headers that interpret it.
steps: #define _POSIX_C_SOURCE selects POSIX declarations.
The headers declare temporary-file creation, read/write/seek, and child waiting. These are interfaces with separate return-value contracts.
walkthrough.change: Changing declarations does not change whether two descriptors share a file position.

walkthrough.title: Own a temporary file
explanation: mkstemp changes the writable name array and returns a descriptor for a newly created file. unlink removes the name while the descriptor retains a reference. Error paths release the descriptor.
walkthrough.question: Why can the program still use a file after unlink?
walkthrough.situation: The parent needs an owned file that disappears when its last open reference closes.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A descriptor names an open entry; removing a pathname does not erase an object that still has open references.
steps: char name[] creates a writable template array.
mkstemp replaces its suffix and returns an open descriptor. Check -1 before using it.
unlink removes only the demo name; close on error releases the open entry.
walkthrough.change: Leaving the name linked requires explicit pathname cleanup later. Do not use a preexisting private file for this demonstration.

walkthrough.title: Counts, errors, and position
explanation: write returns ssize_t: -1 is an error; a nonnegative result is a count. This tiny regular-file demonstration treats a short transfer as an explicit diagnostic, not as an errno error. lseek resets the file position before fork.
walkthrough.question: Why would perror be misleading for a short successful write?
walkthrough.situation: Before creating a child, the parent puts abcd in the file and returns its position to the start.
walkthrough.prerequisite: ssize_t holds either a nonnegative transfer count or -1. The return value must be read before interpreting errno.
steps: write supplies four bytes from the string to fd.
A -1 result reports an error using perror. A nonnegative result other than four reports a short transfer separately.
lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_SET) requests byte position zero. Check its result before forking.
walkthrough.change: Omitting the seek leaves the initial position at the end. A general stream-copy program must handle partial transfers rather than adopting this tiny regular-file assumption.

walkthrough.title: Read in the child
explanation: fork copies descriptor-table entries that refer to the same open file description. sizeof(first) is two because first is a two-byte array here. The child verifies the actual read count and then releases its descriptor.
walkthrough.question: Does closing the child descriptor close the parent entry?
walkthrough.situation: Only the child consumes the first bytes; the parent will observe later.
walkthrough.prerequisite: An array’s sizeof is its total byte size here. read writes into caller-supplied storage and returns a byte count.
steps: fork’s result separates failure, child and parent paths.
char first[2] reserves two bytes; read(fd, first, sizeof(first)) asks for at most those two bytes.
Check -1 separately from a count other than two. Do not treat these two raw bytes as a zero-terminated string.
The child closes its descriptor and ends with _exit. Its read has advanced the shared open-file position.
walkthrough.change: A separate open call would create another open-file description with its own position. Closing one inherited entry does not close the other entry.

walkthrough.title: Establish an observation order
explanation: The parent retries an interrupted wait and checks that the child completed normally. This orders the observation; without it, a race could change which process reads first.
walkthrough.question: Which part of this output depends on waiting?
walkthrough.situation: The parent must observe after the child’s read, rather than racing it.
walkthrough.prerequisite: waitpid both returns a result and writes encoded information through the address &status.
steps: The parent retries waitpid after EINTR because the child may still be running.
After a successful wait, WIFEXITED checks normal termination before WEXITSTATUS checks the child’s success code.
On failure the parent closes its descriptor rather than making the final read look like a valid observation.
walkthrough.change: Removing waiting allows either process to read first, so the experiment would no longer establish this observation order.

walkthrough.title: Read through the remaining reference
explanation: &next is an address where one byte can be stored. The parent descriptor still points to the shared open file description and its current offset. close releases the final demo reference.
walkthrough.question: How would two independent open calls differ from inherited references?
walkthrough.situation: The parent reads one byte at the position left by the child, then releases the last entry.
walkthrough.prerequisite: char next reserves one byte. &next is its address; read needs an address at which to store received bytes.
steps: read(fd, &next, 1) requests one byte into next.
Only a returned count of one makes next a valid observation. -1 and an unexpected count have separate diagnostics.
%c formats a single character; close releases the remaining demo descriptor.
walkthrough.change: Using pread with an explicit offset would avoid changing this open-file description’s current position.

containment.subject: The child and parent
containment.resource: A descriptor referring to the same open file description
containment.operation: Read data and advance the shared offset
containment.enforcement: Descriptor reference semantics; unlink removes only a pathname
containment.remaining: Both processes retain read/write access through surviving descriptors.
containment.establishes: Establishes shared offset state for inherited references. Unlink is not revocation, and the file mode alone is not retested on each read.

lessons.title: Read a child’s termination report
lessons.reading: Read about termination and waiting when you reach those chapters. Keep termination and collecting a child’s status as two separate events.
lessons.summary: A child exits with status 42. What must the parent do to obtain that result?
lessons.prompt: A child exits with status 42. What must the parent do to obtain that result?
explanation: The child ends normally with code 42. The parent needs to learn how that child finished, so it waits for that specific child and collects its completion information. The program prints 42 only after checking that this information describes normal exit.

waitpid has two outputs: its return value identifies the collected child; it writes encoded completion information into storage supplied by the parent. WIFEXITED identifies the normal-exit variant before WEXITSTATUS extracts its code. The walkthrough introduces storage addresses before using &status.

A child stops executing before its parent collects this information. Under this program’s ordinary child-status handling, a zombie is the retained record awaiting collection, not a child still running. The code path uses _exit; library buffering and the different cleanup done by exit are optional deeper reading.
lessons.follow_up: What changes if the child terminates because of a signal instead of calling _exit?
lessons.boundary: waitpid and _exit are application interfaces. The indexed Linux wait and exit implementations are separate layers; architecture and C-library wrappers determine the entry route.

experiment.intro: The child calls _exit(42); the parent handles interrupted waits and decodes a normal exit.
experiment.observe: Notice the normal-exit test before extracting the status.
experiment.assumptions: One owned child, no competing waiter, normal exit with code 42. The parent has not selected a special SIGCHLD disposition.
experiment.variation: Replace _exit(42) with _exit(7). Recompile the complete program; the reported exit status becomes 7. The parent’s own return 0 still means its observation succeeded.
experiment.variability: The actual child PID varies; the displayed comparison stays yes for this single-child program. Exit status is deliberately fixed.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.
The parent collects the child’s status. This program creates no temporary filesystem objects. The parent’s success code differs from the child’s demonstrated code.

checkpoints.title: One part of termination cleanup
checkpoints.notice: This call handles the exiting task’s memory-management context.
checkpoints.ignore: Other cleanup responsibilities can be studied separately.
checkpoints.question: Why is cleanup broader than returning an exit number?

reading.caller: Carries out task termination and its cleanup sequence.
reading.callee: Releases the exiting task’s association with its memory-management context.
reading.statement: do_exit calls exit_mm as one part of termination.
reading.inputs: This call has no explicit arguments. Neighboring calls handle different resources.
reading.result: This statement does not perform the parent’s wait operation or decode an exit status.
reading.syntax: Empty parentheses here supply no arguments. A sequence of call statements delegates separate responsibilities; it is not a proof that every resource has already been released.

checkpoints.title: The parent enters a wait operation
checkpoints.notice: Focus on the wait operation and the surrounding status-handling code.
checkpoints.ignore: Compatibility wrappers and tracing helpers can wait.
checkpoints.question: Which side of the parent-child relationship is waiting here?

reading.caller: Prepares and completes a wait4-style kernel wait request.
reading.callee: Performs the wait operation using the supplied wait options.
reading.statement: kernel_wait4 calls do_wait(&wo), storing its result in ret.
reading.inputs: &wo supplies the address of the prepared wait-options record; fields above select eligible children and requested reports.
reading.result: After releasing the PID reference, a positive result and non-null status address lead to put_user of wo.wo_stat. A copy failure changes ret to -EFAULT.
reading.syntax: & means address. && stops at the first false condition; put_user is reached only after the earlier tests pass. This is kernel code, not the learner’s waitpid wrapper.

next.question: How is a child’s termination cleanup different from collecting its result?

walkthrough.title: Find the interfaces
explanation: errno.h supplies error names; sys/wait.h supplies both the wait interface and macros for interpreting status. A macro looks like a function call here but is expanded by the preprocessor.
walkthrough.question: Which declaration would be missing without sys/wait.h?
walkthrough.situation: A parent will collect completion information from one owned child.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A macro is source-level substitution provided by a header. The WIFEXITED and WEXITSTATUS macros interpret a status value; they do not wait for anything.
steps: unistd.h declares fork and _exit.
sys/wait.h declares waitpid and the status macros. errno.h supplies EINTR for an interrupted wait.
main’s braces contain the whole creation, collection, and report.
walkthrough.change: Removing a status macro does not remove the need to classify the completion information correctly.

walkthrough.title: Create a finite child
explanation: The child path ends with _exit(42). The parent continues; its own eventual return value is a different result. -1 is handled before any attempt to wait for a nonexistent child.
walkthrough.question: Which process returns 42 to whom?
walkthrough.situation: The child has one task: end normally with code 42. The parent needs to collect that result.
walkthrough.prerequisite: fork’s return selects a branch. _exit ends the calling process; it does not stop the other process.
steps: Store the fork result and handle -1 before waiting for a child.
if (child_pid == 0) selects the child; _exit(42) supplies its completion code.
The parent continues after this branch with a positive child PID.
walkthrough.change: Changing the child code changes the collected exit code, not the parent’s PID or the value returned directly by waitpid.

walkthrough.title: Two outputs from one call
explanation: waitpid returns a PID into waited and writes encoded status through &status. A do/while executes at least once. && checks errno only after a failed wait. No status is inspected after a failed wait.
walkthrough.question: Why is status not the returned PID?
walkthrough.situation: The parent cannot report a completion until it has received one.
walkthrough.prerequisite: An address identifies storage. &status lets waitpid write completion information into status; waited stores the call’s separate return value.
steps: int status reserves storage; pid_t waited reserves a PID result.
do executes its body once before while tests whether to repeat.
waitpid(child_pid, &status, 0) blocks for this child. On success waited holds its PID.
&& checks the right-hand condition only when the left is true: inspect errno for EINTR only after -1. Retry that interruption.
A remaining -1 is an error path; do not decode status on that path.
walkthrough.change: Using WNOHANG would add a third result, zero for no available completion; it would require a separate branch, not this blocking-wait interpretation.

walkthrough.title: Classify before extracting
explanation: WIFEXITED selects the normal-exit variant. WEXITSTATUS then extracts that exit code. A child killed by a signal needs WIFSIGNALED and WTERMSIG instead; the normal-exit macro is not a universal decoder.
walkthrough.question: What would you change to describe signal termination?
walkthrough.situation: The collected information must first say which kind of completion occurred.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A variant is one of several meanings carried by encoded data. A decoder for one variant is not valid for all the others.
steps: WIFEXITED(status) checks normal exit.
Only inside that branch does WEXITSTATUS extract 42. %d prints that integer.
The comparison of waited with child_pid yields true/false for the yes/no report; this is distinct from status.
If normal exit was not observed, report failure instead of extracting a normal exit code.
walkthrough.change: Signal termination requires WIFSIGNALED and WTERMSIG, as in the supervision investigation. Termination and collection happen at different times.

containment.subject: The parent’s child
containment.resource: Exit information retained by the kernel
containment.remaining: Waiting does not restrict filesystem access, memory use, or syscalls while the child runs.
containment.establishes: Establishes collection of normal-exit status. A successful wait does not mean the child behaved safely before exit.

lessons.title: Follow a program replacement
lessons.reading: Read the execve discussion and its descriptor behavior when you reach Chapter 27. Compare program replacement with process creation.
lessons.summary: A process successfully executes a new program image. Which would you expect to remain: its PID, an ordinary variable’s changed value, or an unmarked open descriptor?
lessons.prompt: A process successfully executes a new program image. Which would you expect to remain: its PID, an ordinary variable’s changed value, or an unmarked open descriptor?
explanation: The running process first changes value to 42 and prints its ID. It then loads the executable again, with an argument telling the new code to print and finish. This replacement loads new code and initialized data, called a new program image. Its value starts at 7, while the process keeps its ID.
Open descriptors normally survive unless marked close-on-exec or otherwise closed. Exec does not by itself remove every kind of inherited access.

The experiment executes itself with a different argument. Its second run of main shows the same PID and the initial variable value. Code following a successful execl call is not resumed in the old image.
lessons.follow_up: How would a launcher arrange for a helper to receive only the descriptors it needs?
lessons.boundary: execl is a C-library convenience interface. The kernel-side exec path handles the requested replacement; the library-to-kernel transition is a curated conceptual bridge.

experiment.intro: Run the program by its local path. It replaces itself once, using a marker argument.
experiment.expected:
before exec pid=<same ID> value=42
after exec pid=<same ID> value=7
experiment.observe: Compare the two PIDs and the initialization of the ordinary variable.
experiment.assumptions: Run as ./exec_identity from the directory containing the executable. This program does not change directory; argv[0] must remain a usable pathname.
experiment.variation: Replace the string literal "after" with "again" in BOTH strcmp and execl. Leave the longer printed format string unchanged. Recompile; the two lines should still have the same PID and values 42 then 7.
experiment.variability: The PID varies between separate runs, but the before and after IDs match within one successful exec. Values 42 and 7 are controlled by the two image lifetimes.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.
Successful exec replaces this process once. This program creates no child or temporary file; there is nothing to reap or unlink.

checkpoints.title: Preparing a program replacement
checkpoints.notice: Follow the prepared binary-parameter structure into the execution helper.
checkpoints.ignore: Argument copying and security-hook details are further investigations.

reading.statement: do_execveat_common returns the result of bprm_execve(bprm).
reading.inputs: bprm points to the prepared linux_binprm request record; this is not the learner’s raw argv array.
reading.result: return forwards the helper’s result. Inspecting this delegation does not establish that loading will succeed.

walkthrough.title: Program-image initializer
explanation: The file-scope static int is initialized when this program image starts. Headers declare string comparison, output and exec functions.
walkthrough.question: Is initializing this value the same event as creating a PID?
walkthrough.situation: One process will run two successive program images and compare the same named variable.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A program image contains the currently loaded code and data. A file-scope static variable has storage throughout that image’s lifetime. A function argument is an input. At startup, main receives an argument count and access to pointers locating the argument strings; the next segment unpacks that representation.
steps: static int value = 7 gives this image an integer initially containing 7.
The includes supply declarations for output, string comparison and exec.
main receives arguments that tell a newly loaded image which branch to take.
walkthrough.change: A new image initializes its own value even though the process retains its PID. This is distinct from another call to main in the old image.

walkthrough.title: Recognize a new invocation
explanation: argc counts strings; argv is a pointer to an array of pointers to characters. Check the count before indexing argv[1]. strcmp returns zero for equal strings, so this branch tests both count and content.
walkthrough.question: How does && protect the argv[1] access?
walkthrough.situation: The replacement invocation must recognize its marker and avoid replacing itself forever.
walkthrough.prerequisite: argc counts input strings. argv identifies an array of pointers; argv[1] selects the second pointer, then strcmp compares the characters of its string.
steps: argc == 2 first checks that the marker exists.
&& evaluates strcmp only after that count test succeeds.
strcmp returns zero for equal text; == 0 selects the replacement branch.
That branch prints the new image’s value and returns, so it cannot enter the preparation/exec path again.
walkthrough.change: Changing the marker requires changing both this comparison and the string passed to execl. Changing only one can cause repeated replacement.

walkthrough.title: Prepare output before replacement
explanation: The old image changes value to 42 and prints. fflush is checked because exec will discard user-space buffers without flushing them. A successful flush is not a disk-durability guarantee.
walkthrough.question: What output could be lost if fflush were omitted?
walkthrough.situation: The first image changes its variable and needs its message delivered before it is replaced.
walkthrough.prerequisite: printf can keep bytes in a user-space buffer. Exec discards the old image, including such a buffer; it does not perform ordinary stdio cleanup.
steps: value = 42 changes this existing integer.
printf describes the old image and PID; %ld matches the explicit long cast of getpid.
fflush(stdout) sends buffered bytes onward before exec. A returned EOF is failure and stops this path.
walkthrough.change: Removing fflush can lose the before message when redirected. Successful fflush is not proof of durable disk storage.

walkthrough.title: Arguments and the null sentinel
explanation: execl takes a pathname followed by separate argument pointers. The new argv[0] is supplied explicitly. (char *)NULL ends the variable argument list with a pointer of the expected type. The documented ./ command supplies a usable path.
walkthrough.question: Why is a final null pointer different from an empty string?
walkthrough.situation: The current process asks to load the same executable with a marker argument.
walkthrough.prerequisite: An argument is an input to a call. execl accepts individual string pointers and uses a final null pointer to mark the end of that list.
steps: The first argv[0] is the executable pathname; the second supplies the new program’s argument zero.
The string after becomes the new argv[1].
(char *)NULL casts the null value to a character-pointer type suitable for this variable-argument call.
A successful execl replaces the image and continues in its entry path with the same process ID.
walkthrough.change: An empty string is a real argument, not the null pointer that ends the list. The documented ./exec_identity command supplies a usable pathname.

walkthrough.title: The returning path
explanation: Success replaces the image and retains the PID; the after branch observes a freshly initialized value. Only failure returns from execl, so perror belongs on this path.
walkthrough.question: Which instruction is impossible to reach after successful exec?
walkthrough.situation: If exec returns, the existing image remains available to report its error.
walkthrough.prerequisite: perror uses errno from a failed interface call. It belongs after a demonstrated failure, not after successful replacement.
steps: Successful exec never reaches this segment.
A returning execl has failed, so perror describes that failure.
return 1 makes the old invocation report failure to its own parent.
walkthrough.change: Returning zero here would falsely claim success despite a failed replacement.

containment.subject: The process executing a new image
containment.resource: Existing credentials, descriptors, arguments and environment
containment.origin: Retained process context and explicit exec arguments
containment.enforcement: exec image replacement and per-resource transition rules
containment.remaining: The same PID and surviving descriptors remain; exec does not automatically remove authority.
containment.establishes: Establishes image replacement, initializer reset and PID retention. It does not inventory every inherited resource or install a sandbox.

explorer_start.situation: Your C program calls an exec interface to replace its code and data.
