lessons.title: Prepare a launcher
lessons.reading: An optional investigation; it does not advance your book bookmark.
lessons.summary: A launcher supplies a new argument and a small environment, then changes only the child working directory. Which context will the worker see, and what still permits access outside that directory?
lessons.prompt: A launcher supplies a new argument and a small environment, then changes only the child working directory. Which context will the worker see, and what still permits access outside that directory?
explanation: The parent creates an owned work directory and a demo file beside it. Its child changes into work and loads a worker with chosen inputs. The worker measures its actual directory, checks a supplied variable and a deliberately omitted sentinel, and reads the owned file outside work. Disagreement fails the program. The parent separately measures that its directory stayed unchanged.

chdir selects the starting point for relative paths. The successful outside-file read is a concrete counterexample to treating that starting point as a filesystem boundary. The child’s explicit execve arrays choose its argument and environment strings, but leave other authority such as credentials and descriptors unchanged.
lessons.follow_up: Why should cleanup occur after the worker exits?
lessons.boundary: This investigation currently has no reviewed kernel-source checkpoint. Its runtime result and authored explanation remain separate from the compiler index.

experiment.intro: Type or download the complete source, then compile and run as a normal unprivileged Linux user.
experiment.expected:
prepared argument=hello env=worker omitted sentinel=absent
worker cwd matches intended=yes outside demo readable=yes
parent cwd unchanged=yes
experiment.observe: This is expected output, not a record that you personally ran the program.
experiment.assumptions: One thread, one owned child, stable owned /tmp paths, and a usable ./launcher_prepare executable path. No root or host-policy change. Device/inode identity comparisons assume no concurrent replacement of the demo directory.
experiment.variation: Change "hello" to "goodbye" in the arguments array, the worker strcmp validation, and the success output sentence. Recompile. Only the argument report changes; the directory, sentinel and owned outside-file checks must still pass.
experiment.variability: Temporary path names vary. Actual worker directory identity, included DEMO_ROLE, omitted sentinel, outside demo data and unchanged parent cwd are checked before successful completion.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.

Normal completion removes outside, work, then the /tmp/kse-launch-* tree. Abrupt termination can leave that owned tree. Inspect only your generated demo tree before removing it; the experiment never needs a private file.

walkthrough.title: Declarations and feature selection
explanation: _XOPEN_SOURCE requests the declarations used by this POSIX-oriented example. char **argv represents pointers to argument strings.
walkthrough.question: Which declarations require stdlib.h?
walkthrough.situation: A parent will deliberately choose the replacement worker’s arguments, environment and working directory.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A pathname is text used to locate an object. A working directory is the starting point for relative pathname lookup. Neither is the file object itself. A function argument is an input supplied to a call. A pointer is a value locating storage. Each argument string occupies character storage; argv lets main find the pointers to those strings.
steps: _XOPEN_SOURCE requests declarations before headers.
sys/stat.h supplies directory creation and object-identity inspection. stdlib.h supplies environment and allocation interfaces.
int argc holds the argument count. char **argv identifies pointers to argument strings; the worker checks the count before selecting them. These launch inputs are data, not evidence of permission.
walkthrough.change: This example does not change credentials or filesystem permissions outside its owned paths.

walkthrough.title: Interpret explicit launch inputs
explanation: The owned paths are not concurrently renamed in this single-threaded experiment. A production hostile-path launcher needs stronger lifetime/race handling; these observations do not validate that design.
walkthrough.question: What does getenv return when a variable is absent?
walkthrough.situation: The new worker measures its inputs and directory rather than trusting what its launcher intended.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A pointer may be NULL, meaning no object was supplied. Test that before passing it to strcmp. A struct groups named fields; observed.st_ino selects one field.
steps: Check argc before indexing all four supplied inputs. Verify DEMO_ROLE exists and equals worker; verify the parent-only sentinel is absent.
getcwd fills actual with the observed directory pathname. stat retrieves device and inode numbers for actual and the intended path.
Compare both device and inode: together they identify this directory object during our stable, owned experiment. Disagreement returns failure.
fopen opens only the owned outside demo path. fread requests four bytes into a zero-filled array; fclose is attempted before checking the stored results.
Require both the count and content to match demo, and require successful close, before printing success.
walkthrough.change: Omitting chdir must now fail the identity comparison. Passing the whole inherited environment must fail the sentinel test. Reading the outside file establishes that cwd is not a filesystem-access boundary.

walkthrough.title: Resolve paths before changing directory
explanation: realpath produces an allocated absolute executable path; free later releases it. mkdtemp creates a private temporary working directory. getcwd stores the parent directory for comparison.
walkthrough.question: Why resolve argv[0] before chdir?
walkthrough.situation: The parent owns a small temporary tree: a work directory and a demo file beside it.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A function can allocate storage and return its pointer. realpath(..., NULL) does so here; free must later release it. An octal literal such as 0700 describes permission bits.
steps: Resolve the executable before the child changes directory. The documented ./ invocation gives realpath a usable path.
mkdtemp creates the private parent directory; build short suffix paths into PATH_MAX arrays from this bounded template.
mkdir creates work; fopen, fputs and fclose write the owned outside file, retaining both write and close results.
Record the parent’s original cwd. setenv creates only the harmless parent-only sentinel for a later omission test.
On failed preparation, attempt removal of the demo paths and free the allocated executable pathname.
walkthrough.change: The fixed short template makes these suffixes fit; arbitrary input paths would need explicit truncation checks. A cwd change cannot replace credential or pathname access checks.

walkthrough.title: Change only the child context
explanation: fork creates a child; chdir then changes that child only. Errors end the child without running the parent cleanup path.
walkthrough.question: Why does the parent retain its working directory?
walkthrough.situation: The child alone must prepare the worker’s directory; the parent stays in its original directory.
walkthrough.prerequisite: The fork result distinguishes the child’s zero path from the parent’s positive result and a -1 failure. _exit ends only the child.
steps: Store the result in child_pid.
In the zero branch, chdir(working) selects the child’s cwd. A -1 result reports and ends the child.
Only a prepared child proceeds into the exec segment. The parent skips that entire branch and later waits.
walkthrough.change: Changing the parent’s cwd instead would not establish the worker’s intended launch sequence. Removing child chdir is detected by the worker’s actual directory check.

walkthrough.title: Construct pointer arrays
explanation: arguments and environment are null-terminated arrays of string pointers. execve accepts both explicitly, avoiding automatic copying of the whole environment.
walkthrough.question: Is the NULL array terminator an argument the worker can read?
walkthrough.situation: The prepared child must pass chosen inputs instead of implicitly copying every inherited environment string.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A string pointer locates text. An array of string pointers lets execve receive several strings. A final NULL pointer ends the array; it is not a string included in argc.
steps: arguments[] lists executable, marker, hello, intended directory and outside path.
environment[] lists only DEMO_ROLE and PATH; the parent-only sentinel is deliberately absent.
execve takes the executable path, argument-pointer array and environment-pointer array as three inputs.
On success the new image reads these inputs in the worker branch. On failure perror and _exit(1) keep it out of parent cleanup.
walkthrough.change: Passing the inherited environment would restore the sentinel and fail validation. Choosing an environment reduces accidental inputs; it does not remove descriptor or filesystem authority.

walkthrough.title: Reap and release
explanation: The parent waits for its owned child, compares its own directory, removes the empty demo directory and frees the allocated path.
walkthrough.question: Why should cleanup occur after the worker exits?
walkthrough.situation: The parent collects the worker result before removing paths the worker might still need.
walkthrough.prerequisite: wait status is encoded information written through &status. Short-circuit && ensures a normal exit code is extracted only from a normal exit.
steps: Handle fork failure without waiting for a nonexistent child.
Retry waitpid after EINTR. Only on successful collection use WIFEXITED and WEXITSTATUS to set child_ok.
Measure the parent’s cwd independently and compare it to original.
Attempt unlink and both directory removals independently so one failure does not skip the others. free releases the allocated executable path.
Report failure if the worker, parent-cwd check or any cleanup failed.
walkthrough.change: Removing paths before waiting could break the worker observation. Abrupt process termination can leave this owned demo tree; normal execution removes it.

lessons.title: Supervise one child
lessons.reading: An optional investigation; it does not advance your book bookmark.
lessons.summary: The child tells its parent it is ready, then waits. How can the parent stop and collect precisely that child without confusing signal delivery with resource confinement?
lessons.prompt: The child tells its parent it is ready, then waits. How can the parent stop and collect precisely that child without confusing signal delivery with resource confinement?
explanation: The child prepares its signal handling and sends one R byte through a pipe, a channel that carries bytes. The parent waits for that readiness byte before sending SIGTERM only to its owned child. It then waits for completion and verifies that SIGTERM ended that child.

The child deliberately restores default, unblocked SIGTERM and SIGALRM handling so inherited launcher settings do not invalidate the demonstration. Its five-second alarm bounds waiting if the parent fails. Readiness, the termination request and collection of status are three distinct events.
This is lifecycle control, not an access-control policy. A real supervisor also needs a defined response to a worker that catches the signal, and a policy for descendants and bounded waits.
lessons.follow_up: What more would a production supervisor need for a child that catches SIGTERM?

experiment.observe: This is expected output, not a record that you personally ran the program.
experiment.assumptions: Linux and a C compiler. No root or host policy change is needed. The child deliberately sets only its own signal dispositions/mask; a five-second alarm bounds its wait if the parent fails.
experiment.variation: Replace EVERY occurrence of SIGTERM with SIGUSR1 in the complete file: sigaddset, sigaction, kill, WTERMSIG comparison, comments and output label. Keep the SIGALRM fallback unchanged. Recompile. This changes disposition and mask preparation as well as the sent and expected signal; signal only this program’s owned child.
experiment.variability: Child PIDs and scheduling vary. The readiness byte orders setup before the request; the default unblocked termination disposition makes SIGTERM the required collected signal.
troubleshooting: If cc is missing, install your distribution’s ordinary C compiler or use an existing Linux development environment. The browser does not compile code.
Run pwd and ls to confirm that the .c file and executable are in the directory where you are working. The command begins with ./ to execute the local program.
When typing manually, compare the first compiler error with the displayed numbered line. Check semicolons, braces, quotes, header names and the difference between = and ==.
The parent closes its pipe ends and collects the owned child. The child’s five-second alarm bounds its wait if the parent fails. No demo directory is created.

walkthrough.title: Signal and wait interfaces
explanation: The headers declare signal names, pipe and waitpid. The program changes no system-wide settings.
walkthrough.question: Which process ID will be used as a signal target?
walkthrough.situation: A parent will wait for a readiness byte, signal only its owned child, and collect termination information.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A signal is a notification with a configured action, called its disposition. A signal mask can delay delivery. Neither receiving a signal nor requesting one collects wait status.
steps: signal.h declares signal actions and masks.
unistd.h supplies pipe, fork and alarm; sys/wait.h supplies collection and status macros.
_POSIX_C_SOURCE requests the needed declarations before those headers.
walkthrough.change: No host signal policy is changed. Disposition and mask setup below apply to this program’s child.

walkthrough.title: Create a readiness channel
explanation: pipe supplies two descriptor entries. Each branch closes the end it does not need. The one-byte protocol has an exact meaning, not general request framing.
walkthrough.question: Why close the unused write end in the parent?
walkthrough.situation: The parent needs evidence of completed child setup before sending the termination signal.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A pipe supplies two descriptors: index 0 reads; index 1 writes. EOF occurs only when no write-end references remain and buffered bytes have been drained.
steps: int ready[2] reserves two entries for pipe to fill.
pipe(ready) supplies them; check -1 before using them.
fork copies these descriptor references. On fork failure close both parent entries.
The child and parent will each close their unused end, leaving a deliberate one-byte protocol.
walkthrough.change: An arbitrary sleep would not prove readiness. A retained write end can keep a reader waiting for EOF after the real writer exits.

walkthrough.title: Announce readiness
explanation: The child explicitly restores default SIGTERM/SIGALRM dispositions and unblocks them so an inherited shell setting cannot silently make this example wait forever. A five-second alarm is a finite fallback if its parent fails. The checked readiness write, not an arbitrary sleep, tells the parent when setup is complete.
walkthrough.question: Can the signal arrive between the write and pause?
walkthrough.situation: Before announcing readiness, the child establishes how the intended termination signal will behave.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A struct stores named fields. = {0} initializes its members to zero. &action supplies its address to an interface that reads the structure.
steps: action.sa_handler = SIG_DFL chooses default handling. sigemptyset starts empty sets; sigaddset adds SIGTERM and SIGALRM to unblocked.
sigaction restores their default dispositions. sigprocmask removes those signals from this child’s blocked set. Each -1 result fails setup.
alarm(5) schedules a finite fallback termination; it is not the readiness signal.
Close the read end. write sends the R byte from &byte, retrying only EINTR; a successful one-byte count announces completed setup.
Close the write end and pause in a loop. A default terminating signal may end the child even before it reaches pause.
walkthrough.change: Omitting disposition or mask preparation can inherit an ignored or blocked signal. The SIGUSR1 variation must change both preparation and the sent/status-checked signal.

walkthrough.title: Target the owned child
explanation: The parent receives the ready byte, closes the pipe, and calls kill with the child PID. Here SIGTERM may arrive before pause and still terminate the child. Error cleanup also targets only this child.
walkthrough.question: Why is kill(child_pid, SIGTERM) different from signaling a process group?
walkthrough.situation: The parent needs to verify readiness, then request termination from its own child.
walkthrough.prerequisite: read returns a count or -1. A byte’s value is meaningful only after the count proves it was received.
steps: Close the parent’s unused write end so child closure can produce EOF.
read into &byte and retry EINTR. Check both count == 1 and byte == R before considering readiness valid.
Close the read end. Even after a failed handshake, target the owned child for cleanup.
kill(child_pid, SIGTERM) requests delivery to one PID. ESRCH means that target no longer exists; other failures are reported.
walkthrough.change: A negative target could identify a process group and is inappropriate for this demo. Readiness is a specific protocol assertion, not proof of arbitrary worker health.

walkthrough.title: Classify and collect
explanation: WIFSIGNALED selects the signal-termination variant and WTERMSIG identifies SIGTERM. waitpid collects the retained status.
walkthrough.question: What more would a production supervisor need for a child that catches SIGTERM?
walkthrough.situation: Requesting a signal is insufficient: the parent still needs evidence of the child’s termination and must collect its status.
walkthrough.prerequisite: WIFSIGNALED recognizes the signal-termination variant. WTERMSIG extracts its signal number only after that test succeeds.
steps: waitpid blocks for this owned child and retries EINTR.
The || chain stops on failed readiness or a false signal-termination test, protecting the WTERMSIG extraction.
Require SIGTERM before printing the normalized success message. No temporary directory was created by this program.
walkthrough.change: A real worker may catch SIGTERM and continue. This experiment deliberately chooses the default disposition; it is not a general supervisor escalation policy.

lessons.title: Observe one seccomp boundary
lessons.reading: An optional investigation; it does not advance your book bookmark.
lessons.summary: A process can make two identity-related syscalls. If a filter rejects one, what observation would establish that restriction, and which other authority remains?
lessons.prompt: A process can make two identity-related syscalls. If a filter rejects one, what observation would establish that restriction, and which other authority remains?
explanation: The program first requests its parent ID and checks that the request succeeded. It installs a small decision program for numbered kernel requests, then repeats the same request. That request must now fail with EPERM. A separate request for its own ID must still succeed before the program reports success.

Linux calls this decision mechanism seccomp filtering. The optional code walkthrough introduces syscall numbers and the decision program before tracing every instruction. Installation failure, including exit 77, establishes no successful filter execution. A valid zero parent ID is not a failed baseline.

This deny-one policy leaves almost every other native syscall available. It changes neither pathname access rules nor resource limits and is not a complete sandbox. This single-threaded example installs on its calling thread; inheritance and multithreaded scope are explained separately.
lessons.follow_up: What would a deny-one policy fail to say about the rest of the syscall surface?

Requires CONFIG_SECCOMP=y and CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER=y; native aarch64 or x86-64 Linux and headers with seccomp support. An outer policy may deny installation. Exit 77 means unavailable, never a passing mechanism test.

Keep before == -1, because UID zero is valid. Keep native architecture/x32 checks, installation checks and the allowed getpid control unchanged. Recompile the complete file. Replace the baseline comment about a parent outside the PID namespace with "UID zero is valid; it must not be treated as a failed syscall."

This program creates no child or temporary resource. Its thread-local restriction ends when it exits. Exit 77 means installation was unavailable, not that seccomp worked; do not change host policy to force success.

walkthrough.title: Linux interfaces and ABI
explanation: Linux headers define seccomp, classic BPF and audit architecture constants. Only native aarch64 and x86-64 are accepted; syscall numbers cannot be reused blindly across ABIs.
walkthrough.question: Why must the filter check architecture before comparing numbers?
walkthrough.situation: A single-threaded Linux program will deny one native syscall while leaving another available.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A syscall number is the ABI-specific integer identifying a kernel operation. An ABI is the agreed machine-level interface, including how those numbers are interpreted.
steps: _GNU_SOURCE requests syscall and other declarations.
Linux headers define filter instructions and audit architecture tags.
The preprocessor chooses native aarch64 or x86-64 constants; compilation rejects other targets. x32 needs a separate number-bit check even on x86-64.
walkthrough.change: Removing architecture checks can interpret the same number as a different operation. This example is not validated for other architectures.

walkthrough.title: Observe the actual syscall
explanation: syscall(SYS_getppid) bypasses any wrapper caching. The baseline must succeed before an after-filter failure can demonstrate a change.
walkthrough.question: Would an unsupported filter count as a successful restriction test?
walkthrough.situation: The process first checks that the chosen operation can be requested before adding its filter.
walkthrough.prerequisite: syscall is a library interface making the numbered kernel request. Its -1 result signals failure and sets errno. Zero is a value, not automatically an error.
steps: long before stores syscall(SYS_getppid).
if (before == -1) handles actual request failure before claiming a before/after comparison.
A zero parent ID is valid when the parent is outside this caller’s PID namespace; it must pass this check.
walkthrough.change: Using <= 0 incorrectly rejects valid zero. The getuid variation also needs zero to remain valid because UID zero is a legitimate identity value.

walkthrough.title: Read the small decision program
explanation: Load the audit architecture, reject an unexpected ABI, then load the syscall number. On x86-64, reject the alternate x32 number space. The selected number returns EPERM; all remaining native numbers are allowed.
aarch64 denied trace: 0 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 5. Allowed getpid trace: 0 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 6. The nr comparison takes its false jump only for the allowed control.

x86-64 denied trace: 0 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 6 → 7. Allowed getpid trace: 0 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 6 → 8. Both native requests take the false x32-bit branch at instruction 4. These are authored traces of this array, not compiler call edges or runtime traces.
walkthrough.question: Which instructions leave file-opening authority available?
walkthrough.situation: For each request, a small decision program will choose a kernel action. It does not execute these decisions while building the C array.
walkthrough.prerequisite: An array contains elements of one type. struct sock_filter describes one instruction. Classic BPF has a working register holding the most recently loaded value; comparisons inspect that register.
steps: BPF_STMT and BPF_JUMP are C macros that initialize instruction records; | combines opcode bits to describe load, comparison or return.
offsetof(struct seccomp_data, arch) gives the byte offset of the arch field. BPF_ABS loads from that offset in the kernel-supplied request record; it does not follow an arbitrary user pointer.
The architecture comparison chooses whether to skip the kill instruction. The next load replaces the working value with the syscall number.
On x86-64, JSET asks whether the number has bit 0x40000000 set. A set bit identifies the x32 number space and leads to kill.

0x40000000 is a hexadecimal integer literal selecting one binary bit. A bit is one 0-or-1 position in an integer. JSET tests whether any selected bit is 1; it does not ask whether the entire syscall number equals the mask.
The chosen number leads to ERRNO | EPERM; every other native number leads to ALLOW. The numbered tables below trace those paths.
sizeof(instructions) is the array’s byte size. Divide by sizeof(instructions[0]), one element’s byte size, to obtain the instruction count. The small reviewed count fits unsigned short.
.len and .filter name fields of program. The array name supplies a pointer to its first instruction; &program later supplies the address of the whole descriptor.
walkthrough.change: A jump offset counts instructions skipped AFTER the current instruction: target = current index + 1 + offset. Altering it can deny the wrong operation or create an invalid program.

walkthrough.title: Make a one-way local restriction
explanation: The filter applies to the installing thread. Because this process has one thread, that is its entire running code. A multithreaded launcher needs an explicit thread-synchronization design.
no_new_privs does not remove existing permissions, and filters survive allowed fork/exec transitions. Read the linked contracts before generalizing beyond this finite example.
walkthrough.question: Why can the shell continue unaffected after this program exits?
walkthrough.situation: The prepared policy must actually be installed before a denied result can demonstrate this mechanism.
walkthrough.prerequisite: A thread is an execution flow within a process. This example has one. no_new_privs is an irreversible per-thread setting: later exec cannot gain privilege through set-user-ID/set-group-ID file bits or file capabilities. It does not remove existing authority or prevent every credential change using authority already held.
steps: prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1, ...) enables unprivileged filter installation under the documented contract. It is not itself a syscall allowlist.
prctl(PR_SET_SECCOMP, SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER, &program) asks the kernel to validate and attach this program to the calling thread.
Either -1 result prints a diagnostic and exits 77. An unsupported or denied installation is not successful mechanism execution.
walkthrough.change: no_new_privs and attached filters are inherited by children and retained across permitted exec. Existing sibling threads are not synchronized by this prctl; this example does not use seccomp TSYNC. The launching shell is unaffected.

walkthrough.title: Test denied and allowed operations
explanation: The after call must fail with EPERM, and a second actual syscall must still succeed. Both observations are checked before printing success.
walkthrough.question: What would a deny-one policy fail to say about the rest of the syscall surface?
walkthrough.situation: After installation, the program must observe both a denied request and an allowed control before reporting success.
walkthrough.prerequisite: errno is meaningful for this test only after a failed request. && reads left to right and skips later checks after a false condition.
steps: Reset errno, then issue the same numbered getppid request.
after == -1 && errno == EPERM checks the denial’s result and reason together.
A separate SYS_getpid request must return a positive ID; this positive control shows that the policy did not simply stop every request.
Only after both checks does puts print success.
walkthrough.change: The allowed control and deny-one design leave almost all other syscall operations available. No pathname policy, resource limit or complete sandbox has been established.
